events.label:
Leonardo's drawings
in the Codex Madrid I
events.note: An important precursor: in the manuscripts of the Codex Madrid I, Leonardo records observations on mechanics and strength, but does not yet arrive at a complete theory of beams.

events.label: Columbus reaches America
events.note: External chronological reference, included only as a time anchor to show how old the earliest studies in mechanics are.

events.label: Galileo's experiments
events.note: Galileo studies the strength of rods and the fracture of solid bodies: one of the first steps towards a theory of bending, although still based on incorrect assumptions.

events.label:
Jakob Bernoulli:
curvature proportional to M
events.note: In his final work of 1705 he proposes that the curvature of the deformed beam is proportional to the bending moment.

events.label:
Daniel Bernoulli
suggests the energy
approach to Euler
events.note: In a letter of 1742, Daniel Bernoulli suggests to Euler that the elastic curve be treated by means of a strain energy.

events.label:
Euler: correct equation
of the elastic curve
events.note: Euler develops the mathematical theory of the elastic curve and introduces the strain energy per unit length, proportional to the square of the curvature.

events.label:
Daniel Bernoulli:
transverse vibrations
of beams
events.note: The Bernoulli-Euler theory is also applied to the transverse vibrations of beams.

events.label:
Navier: correct theory
of bending
events.note: Navier develops the modern engineering analysis of beams, computing forces and deflections for various supports and load cases.

events.label:
de Saint-Venant:
shear effects
in bending
events.note: His mature contributions on bending and torsion belong mainly to the 1850s; this is where the refinement of the classical theory belongs.

events.label:
Timoshenko beam
(includes shear)
events.note: Conventional date of the theory that includes shear deformation; historically, a first formulation can be traced back to 1916.
